A_target.statement:
Let $\mathbf C$ be a [[Definition:Metacategory|category]] and $A, B$ objects of $\mathbf C$.
A [[Definition:Coproduct|coproduct]] of $A$ and $B$ is an object $A + B$ with morphisms $i_A: A \to A + B$ and $i_B: B \to A + B$ such that for all $f: A \to X$ and $g: B \to X$ there is a [[Definition:Unique|unique]] $u: A + B \to X$ with:
:$u \circ i_A = f, \quad u \circ i_B = g$

B_source.statement:
Let $\mathbf C$ be a [[Definition:Metacategory|category]] and $A, B$ objects of $\mathbf C$.
A [[Definition:Product (Category Theory)|product]] of $A$ and $B$ is an object $A \times B$ with morphisms $\pr_A: A \times B \to A$ and $\pr_B: A \times B \to B$ such that for all $f: X \to A$ and $g: X \to B$ there is a [[Definition:Unique|unique]] $u: X \to A \times B$ with:
:$\pr_A \circ u = f, \quad \pr_B \circ u = g$

object_map.reformulation: Pass to the opposite category C^op, reversing every morphism.

validity_conditions: The universal property of the product is stated purely in terms of morphisms, so reversing all arrows yields a well-formed universal property.
Op is an involution, so the coproduct in C is exactly the product in C^op and vice versa.
proof_plan: Write the [[Definition:Universal Property|universal property]] of the [[Definition:Product (Category Theory)|product]] using only morphisms and commuting triangles.
Reverse every morphism, passing to $\mathbf C^{\text {op} }$.
The projections become injections, and the reversed property is the defining universal property of the [[Definition:Coproduct|coproduct]].

Hence a coproduct in $\mathbf C$ is a product in $\mathbf C^{\text {op} }$.
{{qed}}
